blocks.text: A 28-year-old man has firm, painless swellings along his Achilles tendons and yellowish plaques around his eyelids. His father had a heart attack at 41. A fasting blood test shows a markedly raised LDL cholesterol even though his diet is healthy. Why does a single inherited receptor defect raise the cholesterol in his blood, and how does a drug that blocks one liver enzyme bring it down?

blocks.markdown: **Cholesterol** is a 27-carbon sterol needed to build cell membranes and as the precursor of bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D. Cells obtain it by two routes: synthesis from acetyl-CoA, mainly in the liver, and uptake from lipoproteins carrying dietary and hepatic cholesterol. Because cholesterol is insoluble in water, it travels in blood inside **lipoproteins**, spherical particles with a core of triacylglycerol and cholesteryl ester and a surface of phospholipid, free cholesterol and proteins called **apolipoproteins**.

blocks.title: Rate-limiting step
blocks.text: The rate-limiting step of a pathway is the slowest, most tightly regulated reaction, which controls the flux through the entire pathway. In cholesterol synthesis it is the reduction of HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA) to mevalonate by HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum that uses NADPH.

blocks.markdown:
**Cholesterol synthesis in outline.** Three acetyl-CoA molecules condense to HMG-CoA (cytosolic HMG-CoA synthase). **HMG-CoA reductase** converts it to **mevalonate**, the committed step. Mevalonate is converted by phosphorylation and decarboxylation to five-carbon isoprenoid units, six of which form the 30-carbon **squalene**; squalene cyclises to lanosterol and then, over many steps, to cholesterol.

HMG-CoA reductase is controlled at several levels: (1) when cell cholesterol is low, the transcription factor **SREBP-2** is released from the membrane and switches on the reductase and LDL receptor genes; (2) high sterol levels speed degradation of the reductase protein; (3) insulin favours the active (dephosphorylated) enzyme, while glucagon and AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylate and inactivate it.

blocks.title: Statins
blocks.text: Statins (for example atorvastatin or simvastatin; named here only as pharmacology teaching examples) are structural analogues of HMG-CoA that act as competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase. Lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis lowers the intracellular sterol level, activates SREBP-2 and increases LDL receptor numbers on hepatocytes. More receptors remove more LDL from plasma, which is why plasma LDL falls.

blocks.caption: Cholesterol synthesis: HMG-CoA reductase catalyses the rate-limiting, statin-inhibited step.

blocks.markdown:
**Lipoproteins and their roles.** Lipoprotein classes differ in density, which rises as the proportion of protein increases and triacylglycerol falls. The **exogenous pathway** carries dietary fat: intestinal cells assemble **chylomicrons** (apolipoprotein B-48) carrying dietary triacylglycerol, which enter the blood via lymph. On capillary walls of muscle and adipose tissue, **lipoprotein lipase (LPL)**, activated by apolipoprotein C-II on the particle, hydrolyses triacylglycerol to fatty acids for the tissues. The cholesterol-rich **chylomicron remnant** is taken up by the liver through apolipoprotein E.

The **endogenous pathway** carries lipid made in the liver: **VLDL** (apolipoprotein B-100) carries hepatic triacylglycerol to tissues, where LPL again acts, shrinking it to IDL and then **LDL**, the main cholesterol-carrying particle, which delivers cholesterol to cells via the LDL receptor. **HDL** (built on apolipoprotein A-I) removes excess cholesterol from tissues: the enzyme LCAT esterifies the cholesterol, which is returned to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport).

rows: Delivers dietary fat to muscle and adipose; remnant taken up by liver
Delivers cholesterol to cells through the LDL receptor
Reverse cholesterol transport back to the liver
blocks.caption: Comparison of the four major lipoprotein classes.

blocks.markdown:
**The LDL receptor and familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH).** LDL binds to the LDL receptor on the cell surface (the receptor recognises apolipoprotein B-100), the complex is internalised in clathrin-coated pits by **receptor-mediated endocytosis**, and in lysosomes the cholesteryl ester is hydrolysed to free cholesterol, which suppresses SREBP-2 and therefore cell cholesterol synthesis. The receptor recycles to the surface.

In **familial hypercholesterolaemia**, the commonest cause is a loss-of-function mutation in the LDL receptor gene (an autosomal dominant condition; defects in apolipoprotein B-100 or PCSK9 gain of function cause similar phenotypes). With too few functional receptors, LDL is not cleared from plasma, so LDL cholesterol rises. Two further consequences follow. First, since less cholesterol enters cells by the receptor, cells sense low intracellular cholesterol, SREBP-2 stays active and endogenous synthesis continues unchecked. Second, the excess LDL is oxidised and engulfed by macrophages, producing foam cells, tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus and premature atherosclerosis. Homozygotes are much more severely affected than heterozygotes.

blocks.title: Calculating LDL cholesterol with the Friedewald equation
blocks.prompt: A fasting lipid profile (SI units) gives total cholesterol 6.0 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 1.3 mmol/L and triacylglycerol 1.1 mmol/L. Estimate the LDL cholesterol.

steps.text: The Friedewald equation estimates LDL by subtracting HDL and VLDL cholesterol from total cholesterol, assuming VLDL cholesterol is triacylglycerol divided by 2.2 (in mmol/L). It is valid only for fasting samples with triacylglycerol below about 4.5 mmol/L.
Estimate VLDL cholesterol: 1.1 divided by 2.2 is 0.5 mmol/L.

blocks.answer: Estimated LDL cholesterol is 4.2 mmol/L. Reference ranges and treatment targets vary by laboratory and guideline.

blocks.title: Tracing a fatty meal through the lipoproteins
blocks.prompt: Trace the route of the triacylglycerol in a meal of cheese and the route of cholesterol that the liver exports afterwards, naming the carrier particles and the enzymes that act.

steps.text: Dietary triacylglycerol is digested, absorbed by intestinal cells, repackaged into chylomicrons carrying apolipoprotein B-48, and secreted via lymph into blood.
Lipoprotein lipase, activated by apolipoprotein C-II on the chylomicron, hydrolyses triacylglycerol on muscle and adipose capillaries, releasing fatty acids. The particle shrinks to a remnant.
The liver takes up the chylomicron remnant through apolipoprotein E. The liver later packages triacylglycerol and cholesterol into VLDL (apolipoprotein B-100).
VLDL loses triacylglycerol by the action of LPL, becoming IDL and then LDL, which carries cholesterol to cells and is cleared by LDL receptors.

blocks.answer: Chylomicron (apoB-48, lipoprotein lipase, remnant to liver) then VLDL (apoB-100) then IDL then LDL, which is removed by LDL receptors.

items: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting, SREBP-2 regulated enzyme; statins inhibit it competitively.
Chylomicrons carry dietary triacylglycerol, VLDL endogenous triacylglycerol, LDL cholesterol to tissues and HDL cholesterol back to the liver.
Lipoprotein lipase needs apolipoprotein C-II and acts on chylomicrons and VLDL.
FH usually arises from LDL receptor mutations, so LDL cannot be cleared.

blocks.title: Linking apolipoprotein to function
blocks.text: Remember: B-48 marks chylomicrons (intestine), B-100 marks VLDL, IDL and LDL (liver), A-I activates LCAT on HDL, C-II activates lipoprotein lipase, and E mediates remnant uptake by the liver.

points: HMG-CoA reductase makes mevalonate and is the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis; statins are competitive inhibitors that raise hepatic LDL receptor number.
Chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL and HDL carry dietary fat, liver fat, cholesterol to tissues and cholesterol back to the liver respectively.
LDL is cleared by receptor-mediated endocytosis, and loss of functional LDL receptors causes familial hypercholesterolaemia with raised LDL, xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis.
LDL cholesterol can be estimated by the Friedewald equation from fasting total cholesterol, HDL and triacylglycerol.

questions.stem: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step of cholesterol biosynthesis?

options.text: HMG-CoA reductase
HMG-CoA synthase
Lipoprotein lipase
Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate and is the regulated, rate-limiting enzyme.
distractorRationale.b: HMG-CoA synthase makes HMG-CoA, an earlier step that is not rate limiting for cholesterol.
distractorRationale.c: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triacylglycerol in lipoproteins and is not in the synthesis pathway.
distractorRationale.d: LCAT esterifies cholesterol on HDL; it is not part of synthesis.

questions.explanation: HMG-CoA reductase produces mevalonate, the committed step, and is regulated by SREBP-2, sterol-accelerated degradation and phosphorylation. It is the target of statins. The other enzymes act in different parts of metabolism.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with high LDL cholesterol is started on a statin. Which is the best explanation of why her plasma LDL cholesterol falls?

options.text: Lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis increases LDL receptor expression, so more LDL is cleared from plasma
The drug blocks intestinal chylomicron formation so no cholesterol is absorbed
The drug activates lipoprotein lipase to hydrolyse LDL
The drug converts cholesterol directly into bile acids in the plasma

questions.correctOptionText: Lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis increases LDL receptor expression, so more LDL is cleared from plasma

distractorRationale.a: Correct: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition lowers intracellular sterol, activating SREBP-2 and LDL receptor synthesis.
distractorRationale.b: Statins do not prevent chylomicron assembly.
distractorRationale.c: Lipoprotein lipase acts on triacylglycerol in chylomicrons and VLDL, and statins do not activate it.
distractorRationale.d: Bile acid synthesis occurs in hepatocytes, not in plasma, and is not the statin mechanism.

questions.explanation: A statin competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, so the hepatocyte senses low cholesterol and activates SREBP-2, which increases LDL receptors. The extra receptors remove more LDL from the circulation, lowering plasma LDL cholesterol.

questions.stem: Blood taken from a patient 2 hours after a high-fat meal is milky. Which lipoprotein is mainly responsible for the milky appearance?

options.text: Chylomicrons
LDL
HDL
IDL

distractorRationale.a: Correct: large, triacylglycerol-rich chylomicrons scatter light and carry dietary fat after a meal.
distractorRationale.b: LDL particles are small and cholesterol rich; they do not make plasma milky.
distractorRationale.c: HDL particles are small and dense.
distractorRationale.d: IDL is a transient intermediate between VLDL and LDL, small in concentration.

questions.explanation: After a fatty meal, intestinal cells secrete large triacylglycerol-rich chylomicrons that scatter light and give lipaemic plasma. They are cleared by lipoprotein lipase and the liver over several hours.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the main role of HDL?

options.text: It collects cholesterol from tissues, esterified by LCAT, and returns it to the liver
It carries dietary triacylglycerol from the intestine to muscle
It carries liver-made triacylglycerol to adipose tissue
It delivers cholesterol to peripheral cells through the LDL receptor

questions.correctOptionText: It collects cholesterol from tissues, esterified by LCAT, and returns it to the liver

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is reverse cholesterol transport, driven by apoA-I and LCAT.
distractorRationale.d: This describes LDL, whose apoB-100 binds the LDL receptor.

questions.explanation: HDL, built around apolipoprotein A-I, takes up cholesterol from peripheral cells. LCAT converts it to cholesteryl ester, which is delivered to the liver. Triacylglycerol is carried mainly by chylomicrons and VLDL, and LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues.

questions.stem: In a child with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia with no functional LDL receptors, what would you expect for hepatic cholesterol synthesis compared with a healthy child?

options.text: Not suppressed, because little LDL cholesterol enters hepatocytes to suppress SREBP-2 and HMG-CoA reductase
Suppressed, because the high plasma LDL inhibits HMG-CoA reductase directly in hepatocytes
Absent, because LDL is needed to supply acetyl-CoA
Reduced, because mevalonate cannot be made without LDL receptors

questions.correctOptionText: Not suppressed, because little LDL cholesterol enters hepatocytes to suppress SREBP-2 and HMG-CoA reductase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: feedback depends on cholesterol entering the cell via the receptor.
distractorRationale.b: High plasma LDL cannot enter cells without receptors, so it cannot suppress the enzyme.
distractorRationale.c: Acetyl-CoA comes from cell metabolism, not LDL.
distractorRationale.d: Mevalonate synthesis does not depend on receptor function; it is unchecked.

questions.explanation: Feedback regulation of HMG-CoA reductase works through cholesterol that enters the cell via LDL receptors. Without receptors, hepatocytes sense low cholesterol and SREBP-2 stays active, so synthesis continues while plasma LDL is already very high.

questions.stem: True or false: VLDL is assembled in the liver and carries apolipoprotein B-100.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The liver assembles VLDL around apolipoprotein B-100 to export endogenous triacylglycerol. Chylomicrons, in contrast, are made in the intestine and carry apolipoprotein B-48.

questions.stem: A fasting lipid profile gives total cholesterol 7.8 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 1.1 mmol/L and triacylglycerol 2.2 mmol/L. Use the Friedewald equation (VLDL cholesterol = triacylglycerol divided by 2.2, in mmol/L) to estimate LDL cholesterol in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: VLDL cholesterol is 2.2 divided by 2.2 = 1.0 mmol/L. LDL cholesterol equals total cholesterol minus HDL minus VLDL cholesterol: 7.8 - 1.1 - 1.0 = 5.7 mmol/L. The equation assumes a fasting sample and triacylglycerol below about 4.5 mmol/L.

questions.stem: Compare the origins, main apolipoproteins and functions of chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL and HDL in lipid transport.
markingGuide: Chylomicrons: made in intestine, apoB-48, carry dietary triacylglycerol; lipoprotein lipase (activated by apoC-II) releases fatty acids; remnant taken up by liver
VLDL: made in liver, apoB-100, carries endogenous triacylglycerol to tissues; lipoprotein lipase reduces it to IDL and LDL
LDL: derived from VLDL, apoB-100, main cholesterol carrier; delivers cholesterol to cells via the LDL receptor
HDL: apoA-I, picks up tissue cholesterol, LCAT esterifies it, returns it to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport)
Distinguishes triacylglycerol carriers (chylomicron, VLDL) from cholesterol carriers (LDL, HDL)
questions.explanation: Chylomicrons and VLDL carry triacylglycerol, from diet and liver respectively, while LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues and HDL returns it to the liver. Each is distinguished by its apolipoproteins and tissue of origin.

questions.stem: Explain, step by step, how a loss-of-function mutation in the LDL receptor gene leads to the raised LDL cholesterol, tendon xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia.
markingGuide: Normally LDL binds the LDL receptor (through apoB-100) and is internalised by receptor-mediated endocytosis in clathrin-coated pits
Lysosomal hydrolysis releases free cholesterol, which suppresses SREBP-2 and cholesterol synthesis; the receptor recycles
With fewer functional receptors, LDL clearance from plasma falls and plasma LDL cholesterol rises
Low intracellular cholesterol in the cell keeps HMG-CoA reductase active so synthesis continues
Excess LDL is oxidised and taken up by macrophages as foam cells, producing xanthomas and atheromatous plaques, hence premature coronary disease
Autosomal dominant; homozygotes are more severely affected than heterozygotes
questions.explanation: A defective receptor slows LDL uptake, so LDL accumulates in plasma and is deposited in tissue by macrophages as cholesterol-laden foam cells. These deposits form tendon xanthomas and drive early atherosclerosis. Meanwhile feedback inhibition of hepatic synthesis fails because too little cholesterol enters the cell.

questions.stem: What is the action of lipoprotein lipase on chylomicrons and VLDL?

options.text: It hydrolyses their triacylglycerol, releasing fatty acids for uptake by tissues
It esterifies free cholesterol on their surface
It binds them to the LDL receptor
It synthesises their apolipoproteins

questions.correctOptionText: It hydrolyses their triacylglycerol, releasing fatty acids for uptake by tissues

distractorRationale.a: Correct: LPL, activated by apoC-II, hydrolyses core triacylglycerol on capillary walls.
distractorRationale.b: Esterification of cholesterol is carried out by LCAT.
distractorRationale.c: Binding to the LDL receptor is mediated by apolipoproteins B-100 and E.
distractorRationale.d: Apolipoproteins are made by the liver and intestine, not by LPL.

questions.explanation: Lipoprotein lipase sits on capillary endothelium and, activated by apolipoprotein C-II, hydrolyses triacylglycerol to fatty acids and glycerol. This shrinks chylomicrons to remnants and VLDL to IDL and LDL.
